module.title: Defining Relative Clauses: Who, Which, That & Where
module.group: A2.3 - World Explorations, Stories & Bridge to B1
module.objective: Add concise descriptive detail to people, objects, and places using defining relative pronouns (who, which, that, where).

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Discovering History and Famous Places
subModules.grammarFocus: Defining Relative Clauses (Who, Which, That, Where)

content.summary: In this reading mission, you will explore short texts about museums, ancient monuments, and famous inventions. You will learn how to connect two ideas into one smooth sentence using relative pronouns like who, which, that, and where.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Defining relative clauses using who for people, which and that for things, and where for places.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Key terms related to history, architecture, science, and museum exhibits.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning texts to identify specific definitions and relative pronouns that describe nouns.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea and key details of short A2 texts about historical places and inventions.
Recognize how relative clauses give extra information about people, things, and places.
Practice identifying relative pronouns in descriptive reading passages.

contextWarmup.prompt: What is the best way to learn about ancient history?
options: Visiting a museum where old artifacts are displayed
Reading a recipe book in the kitchen
Watching a cartoon about modern technology
contextWarmup.explanation: Museums are places where people go to see ancient artifacts and learn about history.

rules: WHO: Used for people. Formula: noun (person) + who + verb or clause. Example: 'An architect is someone who designs buildings.'
WHICH / THAT: Used for things or animals. Formula: noun (thing) + which/that + verb or clause. Example: 'Egypt is a country which has many ancient monuments.'
WHERE: Used for places. Formula: noun (place) + where + subject + verb. Example: 'A gallery is a place where artists display their paintings.'

commonTrap.explanation: Students often mix up who and which, or use where for things instead of places.
commonTrap.wrong: This is the museum who I visited yesterday.
commonTrap.correct: This is the museum which I visited yesterday, or this is the city where I live.

content.contractionsSubtitle: Observe how subjects and verbs smoothly merge in everyday English:

contractions.subject: That
contractions.exampleFull: That is the monument which we saw yesterday.
contractions.exampleContracted: That's the monument which we saw yesterday.

contractions.subject: It
contractions.exampleFull: It is a temple where people pray.
contractions.exampleContracted: It's a temple where people pray.

paragraphs: Welcome to the Global History Museum, which is a fantastic place where visitors can learn about the past. An architect named Thomas designed this amazing building in the nineteenth century. Inside the halls, you can see every ancient artifact that people discovered during old expeditions around the world. Every explorer who traveled across deserts and mountains left special items here.

Another popular section is the science gallery, which displays famous inventions that changed human life. A scientist works in this area to show how machines operate. Visitors love walking through the sculpture room, where local artists show their creative work. If you want to understand history, this museum is a building that you must visit.

sections.title: Audio Dialogue: Planning Our City Tour

content.context: Sarah and Tom discuss their weekend plans to visit a museum, a gallery, and a local café using defining relative clauses.
content.audioPrompt: Listen to the conversation between Sarah and Tom.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: I want to visit the new museum.
lines.translation: Aku ingin mengunjungi museum baru itu.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: It is the place that opened recently.
lines.translation: Itu adalah tempat yang baru saja dibuka.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Is there a guide who knows history?
lines.translation: Apakah ada pemandu yang tahu sejarah?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Yes, a historian works in that gallery.
lines.translation: Ya, seorang sejarawan bekerja di galeri itu.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: She is the person that explains ancient artifacts.
lines.translation: Dia adalah orang yang menjelaskan artefak kuno.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: They have a room where you see armor.
lines.translation: Mereka punya ruangan di mana kamu melihat baju zirah.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: That sounds like a place which is amazing.
lines.translation: Itu terdengar seperti tempat yang luar biasa.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: After that, let us visit the old café.
lines.translation: Setelah itu, mari kita kunjungi kafe lama.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Is it the shop which sells sweet pastries?
lines.translation: Apakah itu toko yang menjual kue manis?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Yes, the chef who bakes them is friendly.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: We can meet friends who love local food.
lines.translation: Kita bisa menemui teman-teman yang suka makanan lokal.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Let us go there this afternoon together.
lines.translation: Mari kita pergi ke sana sore ini bersama.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Defining Relative Clauses with Who, Which, That, and Where

content.summary: Learn how to connect two ideas into one clear sentence using relative pronouns like who, which, that, and where to describe people, things, and places.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Using 'Who' for People
blueprintItems.example: The man who lives next door is a teacher.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Using 'Which' and 'That' for Things
blueprintItems.example: I want a computer which has a fast processor.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Using 'Where' for Places
blueprintItems.example: This is the park where we play football on Sundays.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not use commas before or after defining relative clauses.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The woman, who works at the bank, is my aunt.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The woman who works at the bank is my aunt.
mechanicsRules.why: Defining relative clauses give essential information, so commas are not needed.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'who' only for people, never for things or places.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The car who is parked outside is red.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The car which is parked outside is red.
mechanicsRules.why: Relative pronoun 'who' is strictly for human subjects.

mechanicsRules.rule: Ensure correct subject-verb agreement inside the relative clause.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I like friends who is kind and helpful.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I like friends who are kind and helpful.
mechanicsRules.why: The verb in the relative clause must agree with the noun it describes.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Describe Your Best Friend
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three sentences about your best friend using 'who'. Mention their name, what they look like or do, and why you like them.
guidedLabChallenges.example: My best friend is Sarah who has long brown hair. She is a person who always helps me with homework. We like playing tennis together.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Describe Your Favorite Place
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three sentences about your favorite place using 'where'. Mention the name of the place, where it is, and what you do there.
guidedLabChallenges.example: Central Park is the place where I go every weekend. It is a big park where people walk their dogs. I love sitting under the trees and reading.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the two sentences into one using 'who': 'A baker is a person. This person makes bread.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: A baker is a person + [who] + makes bread.
practicumQuestions.hint: Connect the noun and relative pronoun directly.
targetAnswers: A baker is a person who makes bread.
A baker is someone who makes bread.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'who' after 'person' to describe human professions.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the two sentences using 'which': 'I bought a camera. The camera takes great photos.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: I bought a camera + [which] + takes great photos.
targetAnswers: I bought a camera which takes great photos.
I bought a camera that takes great photos.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'which' or 'that' for inanimate objects like cameras.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the two sentences using 'where': 'This is the cafe. We drink coffee there.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: This is the cafe + [where] + we drink coffee.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'where' to replace the location reference.
targetAnswers: This is the cafe where we drink coffee.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'where' to refer to a specific location or place.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence with the correct relative pronoun (who, which, or where): 'The girl ______ won the competition is my sister.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: The girl ______ won the competition is my sister.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'who' (or 'that' in informal contexts) for people.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence with the correct relative pronoun: 'Show me the shop ______ you bought your bicycle.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: Show me the shop ______ you bought your bicycle.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'where' when talking about locations where actions happen.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalization and punctuation error in this relative clause sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: the man who repair cars is very honest
practicumQuestions.hint: Check the first letter, verb agreement, and ending punctuation.
targetAnswers: The man who repairs cars is very honest.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Capitalize the first letter, use 'repairs' for third-person singular, and add a period.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Verify if this sentence is correct: 'I lost the umbrella that my mother gave me.' Type 'Yes' or rewrite correctly.
practicumQuestions.promptText: I lost the umbrella that my mother gave me.
targetAnswers: I lost the umbrella that my mother gave me.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Umbrellas are things, so 'that' or 'which' is correct.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a complete sentence defining a teacher using 'who'.
practicumQuestions.hint: Complete the clause with an action teachers do.
targetAnswers: A teacher is someone who teaches students.
A teacher is a person who teaches students.
A teacher is someone who helps students learn.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A defining relative clause with 'who' correctly identifies a person's role.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine: 'She wears a jacket. The jacket has red buttons.'
practicumQuestions.promptText: She wears a jacket + [which/that] + has red buttons.
targetAnswers: She wears a jacket which has red buttons.
She wears a jacket that has red buttons.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Both 'which' and 'that' are correct for describing things.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a sentence defining a kitchen using 'where'.
practicumQuestions.promptText: A kitchen is a room where...
practicumQuestions.hint: What do people do in a kitchen?
targetAnswers: A kitchen is a room where people cook food.
A kitchen is a place where people cook meals.
A kitchen is a room where food is cooked.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'where' to describe what activity takes place in a specific room or place.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Defining Relative Clauses and Places

content.summary: Learn how to speak clearly using defining relative clauses to describe people, things, and places without pausing awkwardly.
content.audioGuidance: Focus on linking words together and using natural pausing before relative pronouns like who, which, that, and where.

pillars.name: Relative Pronunciation
pillars.explanation: Pronounce words like who, which, that, and where softly in sentences, keeping the main stress on important nouns and verbs.

pillars.name: Sentence Flow
pillars.explanation: Avoid stopping between the main clause and the relative clause so your speech sounds natural.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice that the main stress moves to the third syllable when the word becomes an adjective.
Notice that the stress shifts to the third syllable in the related adjective form.
Notice that the stress moves to the middle syllable in the adjective form.
Notice that the main stress shifts to the second syllable in the plural form.

practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your friend asks: 'Did you see that strange metal object in the first room?' Respond using a defining relative clause with 'that'.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yes, that is an artifact that people made thousands of years ago.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /jɛs ðæt ɪz ən ˈɑːtɪfækts ðæt ˈpiːpl meɪd/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'that' to define things clearly in conversation.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are speaking with a tour guide about famous inventors and scientists.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Curious Tourist asking about historical figures
practicumQuestions.instruction: Ask the guide about an architect who designed old buildings.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Ask your tour guide to explain who designed the local town hall.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Can you tell me who the architect was that designed this building?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /kæn juː tɛl miː huː ði ˈɑːkɪtɛkt wɒz ðæt dɪˈzaɪnd/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'who' or 'that' when asking about people.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are discussing historic places with a classmate for a school project.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Student working on a history assignment
practicumQuestions.instruction: Describe a gallery where art is displayed.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your partner asks where you want to meet to study. Suggest the art gallery using 'where'.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: We should meet at the gallery where local painters display their artwork.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wiː ʃʊd miːt æt ðə ˈɡæləri weə ˈloʊkəl ˈpeɪntəz dɪˈspleɪ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'where' to refer to places in conversation.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are talking about technology and modern inventions with a teacher.
practicumQuestions.instruction: Explain an invention that changed communication using 'which'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your teacher asks: 'What is an invention which changed how we talk to people?' Answer using 'which'.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The smartphone is an invention which allows us to talk to anyone instantly.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə ˈsmɑːtfəʊn ɪz ən ɪnˈvenʃn wɪtʃ əˈlaʊz ʌs tuː tɔːk/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'which' to talk about things.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Pronounce the target vocabulary word clearly with correct syllable stress.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say the word 'explorer' and use it in a sentence with 'who'.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: An explorer is someone who travels to discover new places.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ən ɪkˈsplɔːrər ɪz ˈsʌmwʌn huː ˈtrævəlz tuː dɪsˈkʌvər nuː pleɪsɪz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Focus on pronouncing 'explorer' with stress on the second syllable.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practice a defining relative clause sentence combining two ideas.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Read aloud this sentence using 'where' correctly.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: This is the century where technology grew very fast.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðɪs ɪz ðə ˈsentʃəri weə tɛkˈnɒlədʒi ɡruː ˈvɛri fɑːst/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Ensure 'where' correctly connects the noun 'century' to the relative clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practice correct word stress on multi-syllable nouns.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say the word 'monument' and read the sentence clearly.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: A monument is a structure which people build to remember important events.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ə ˈmɒnjumənt ɪz ə ˈstrʌktʃə wɪtʃ ˈpiːpl bɪld tuː rɪˈmembər/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Emphasize the first syllable of 'monument'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Use falling intonation at the end of a descriptive statement with a relative clause.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Read this statement with a clear falling tone at the end.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Egypt is a country which has many ancient monuments.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈiːdʒɪpt ɪz ə ˈkʌntri wɪtʃ hæz ˈmeni ˈeɪnʃənt ˈmɒnjumənts/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Lower your pitch at the end of the sentence to show completion.
